lesson.title: Alternative names in the passage
lesson.text: A passage may give two names for the same feature: "a cirque, also known as a corrie". Either name can usually be accepted if it fits the word limit, but the label may already contain one of them. Also watch for adjectives that separate similar features, such as "lateral" (at the side) and "terminal" (at the end).
lesson.example: Passage: "the estuary, or river mouth". Label: "(1) ______: where the river meets the sea". Answer: estuary / river mouth.

questions.evidence: a cirque, also known as a corrie, a deep, armchair-shaped hollow.
questions.explanation: Both names are given in the passage and fit the limit.

questions.evidence: its accumulation zone, where more snow falls each year than melts.
questions.explanation: The gap is followed by "than melts", so it needs a subject and verb: "snow falls".

questions.evidence: forming crevasses, deep cracks in the ice that can be dangerous ... because they are often hidden by snow.
questions.explanation: The label is the definition.

questions.evidence: Rock that has fallen from the valley sides collects along the edges of the glacier, forming a ridge known as a lateral moraine.
questions.explanation: "Moraine" is already in the label. A medial moraine runs down the middle, not along the edges.

questions.evidence: the glacier loses more ice than it gains, mainly by melting, but also by evaporation.
questions.explanation: "Mainly" points to melting, not evaporation.

questions.evidence: The front edge of the glacier, where the ice ends, is known as the snout.
questions.explanation: The label is the definition.

questions.evidence: a terminal moraine, often marks the furthest advance of the ice.
questions.explanation: "Of the ice" is already in the label.

lesson.title: Circular diagrams: from outside to centre
lesson.text: A circular cross-section, such as a tree trunk, the Earth or a cable, is arranged in rings from the outside to the centre. The passage usually describes them in the same order, using words such as "just inside", "beneath this" and "at the very centre". Match each ring in turn, and be careful with rings that have similar functions but carry different substances.
lesson.example: Passage: "A cable has a plastic coating; beneath it is a copper wire." Outer ring: "plastic (1) ______". Answer: coating.

questions.evidence: the outer bark, a layer of dead cells that protects the living tissue inside.
questions.explanation: "Outer" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: the inner bark, also known as the phloem ... carries sugars ... down to the rest of the tree.
questions.explanation: "Inner bark" is two words, over the limit of ONE WORD, so the alternative name "phloem" must be used.

questions.evidence: the cambium, a layer so thin that it can barely be seen. It is, however, where growth takes place: its cells divide.
questions.explanation: "New cells produced here" paraphrases "its cells divide".

questions.evidence: This pale, living layer carries water and minerals upwards.
questions.explanation: The phloem carries sugars downwards; the sapwood carries water upwards.

questions.evidence: it is very hard and gives the tree its support.
questions.explanation: "Gives the tree" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: At the very centre of the trunk is the pith, a small area of soft tissue.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: The result is a visible growth ring for each year of the tree's life.
questions.explanation: "For each year" means one ring shows one year of growth.

lesson.title: When left and right are reversed
lesson.text: Anatomical diagrams are drawn as if you are facing the person, so the heart's right side appears on the left of the page, and its left side on the right. Hard passages expect you to notice this. Rely on the labels that are already complete (such as "right atrium") rather than on the side of the page, and check each answer against the passage's description of function, not position alone.
lesson.example: Diagram of a person facing you: label on the left of the page, "(1) ______ hand holding a pen". Passage: "She writes with her right hand." Answer: right.

questions.evidence: The right ventricle then pumps the blood into the pulmonary artery, which carries it to the lungs.
questions.explanation: "Oxygen-poor" matches "the only artery ... that carries oxygen-poor blood". The aorta carries oxygen-rich blood to the body.

questions.evidence: a small group of cells in the wall of the right atrium called the sinoatrial node, often described as the heart's natural pacemaker.
questions.explanation: "Natural pacemaker" also fits the limit, but "pacemaker" is already in the label, so the name is required.

questions.evidence: passes down into the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve, whose three flaps close to prevent blood flowing backwards.
questions.explanation: The label is on the right side of the heart (left of the page). The mitral valve is on the left side.

questions.evidence: the aorta, the largest artery in the body.
questions.explanation: This label is on the heart's left side, next to the left ventricle, which pumps blood into it.

questions.evidence: Blood from the lungs returns to the left atrium.
questions.explanation: The right atrium receives blood from the body, not from the lungs.

questions.evidence: The two sides of the heart are completely separated by a thick muscular wall called the septum.
questions.explanation: This is the definition. "Hole in the heart" describes a fault in the septum, not the wall itself.

questions.evidence: its muscular walls are about three times thicker than those of the right ventricle.
questions.explanation: "Three" alone does not fit grammatically before "thicker"; "times" is needed.

lesson.title: Figures and parts in the same label
lesson.text: Hard labels may combine a part with a figure: "(2) ______ produces about (3) ______ of the thrust". Such labels contain two gaps from the same sentence, one a name and one a number. Read the whole sentence, identify which word in the passage matches each gap, and include units (per cent, times, metres) only if they are not already in the label.
lesson.example: Label: "(1) ______: about (2) ______ of the total". Passage: "Wheat accounts for about 40 per cent of the total." Answers: wheat; 40 per cent.

questions.evidence: the fan at the front, a ring of large, curved blades that can be more than three metres in diameter.
questions.explanation: "Can exceed" paraphrases "can be more than".

questions.evidence: Most of it, known as bypass air, flows around the core of the engine.
questions.explanation: "Flows around the core" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: this bypass air produces about 80 per cent of the thrust.
questions.explanation: The unit must be included because it is not in the label.

questions.evidence: it is at up to 40 times its original pressure.
questions.explanation: "Original pressure" is already in the label; "40 times" or "40 times its" both fit the limit.

questions.evidence: The compressed air then enters the combustion chamber, where it is mixed with fuel and burned. The temperature here can reach 1,500°C.
questions.explanation: The turbine is driven by hot gases but is not where the fuel burns.

questions.evidence: The turbine is connected by a long central shaft to the compressor and the fan.
questions.explanation: "Long central shaft" is exactly three words, so it is within the limit; "shaft" alone is also acceptable.

questions.evidence: the gases leave through the exhaust nozzle at the back of the engine.
questions.explanation: "Gases leave" is already in the label.

lesson.title: Word banks where both directions are used
lesson.text: In some hard sets, both an option and its opposite are correct answers, for different labels. "Rises" may be correct in one layer and "falls" in another. Do not cross out an opposite just because its partner has been used. Decide each gap independently from the passage.
lesson.example: Passage: "Prices rose in spring and fell in autumn." Labels: "spring: prices (1) ______", "autumn: prices (2) ______". Options: A rose B fell. Answers: A, B.

questions.evidence: The exosphere gradually merges with space.
questions.explanation: J (gravity) is mentioned in the paragraph, but some particles escape gravity; the layer does not merge with it.

questions.evidence: The thermosphere is where auroras occur.
questions.explanation: H (satellites) do not "occur"; the space station, already in the label, is the only orbiting object mentioned.

questions.evidence: Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.evidence: the ozone layer, which absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
questions.explanation: I (ozone) is already in the label; it is what does the absorbing.

questions.evidence: Here, the pattern is reversed: the temperature rises with height.
questions.explanation: In the stratosphere, temperature increases, the opposite of the troposphere.

questions.evidence: it is where almost all weather happens.
questions.explanation: The verb "happens" fits "weather".

questions.evidence: In the troposphere, the temperature falls with height.
questions.explanation: Both E and F are used: each is correct for a different layer.

lesson.title: Long layered diagrams with mixed answer types
lesson.text: A detailed cross-section may have eight or more labels, and the answers may include materials, numbers with units, names of parts and substances. Hard passages also describe the layers in construction order (from the bottom up), while the diagram is labelled from the top down. Number the passage paragraphs against the diagram before you start answering.
lesson.example: Passage: "First a gravel base was laid, then paving stones on top." Diagram (top first): "paving stones", "(1) ______ base". Answer: gravel.

questions.evidence: the cap is covered with topsoil and planted with grass.
questions.explanation: "Topsoil" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: it is sealed with a cap. The cap usually consists of another layer of clay, which keeps rainwater out.
questions.explanation: "Clay" is already in the label, so the answer is the name of the layer.

questions.evidence: at the end of the day it is covered with around fifteen centimetres of soil.
questions.explanation: "About 15 cm" is already in the label. "Daily cover" is the name of the layer, but the label asks for the material.

questions.evidence: The gas is removed through vertical wells that are drilled down into the waste.
questions.explanation: "Vertical" is already in the label. "Monitoring wells" are a different kind of well, used to test groundwater.

questions.evidence: a network of perforated pipes ... collect the leachate that trickles down through the waste.
questions.explanation: "Pipes collect" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: a plastic liner, a sheet of high-density polyethylene around two millimetres thick.
questions.explanation: The unit is not in the label, so it must be included. "One metre" is the thickness of the clay layer.

questions.evidence: the natural ground is covered with a layer of compacted clay about one metre thick.
questions.explanation: This is the lowest layer of the base; the passage describes the base from the bottom up.

questions.evidence: Beneath the site, groundwater is regularly tested through monitoring wells.
questions.explanation: "Tested through monitoring wells" is already in the label.

lesson.title: A group name or an individual name?
lesson.text: When a passage gives a group name and then the names of its members ("the ossicles: the hammer, the anvil and the stirrup"), check whether the label refers to the whole group or to one member. Numbers in the label ("three ______") point to the group; a description that fits only one item ("the smallest bone") points to the individual.
lesson.example: Passage: "The three primary colours are red, yellow and blue." Label: "three (1) ______". Answer: primary colours (not red).

questions.evidence: The pinna collects sound waves and directs them into the canal.
questions.explanation: "Collects sound waves" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: lined with small glands that produce wax.
questions.explanation: "Glands produce" is already in the label. "Dust" is what the wax traps.

questions.evidence: the eardrum, a thin, tight membrane that vibrates when sound waves strike it.
questions.explanation: The label describes the eardrum; the answer is its name.

questions.evidence: three tiny bones, known collectively as the ossicles ... Together, they pass the vibrations of the eardrum inwards, increasing their force about twenty times.
questions.explanation: "Three" and "together" point to the group name, not one bone such as the "stirrup".

questions.evidence: providing the brain with the information it needs to maintain the body's sense of balance.
questions.explanation: The passage says these canals have "nothing to do with hearing", so "hearing" is wrong.

questions.evidence: the cochlea, a snail-shaped tube coiled two and a half times and filled with fluid.
questions.explanation: The semicircular canals are also fluid-filled, but they are loops, not snail-shaped.

questions.evidence: the Eustachian tube, which equalises the air pressure on either side of the eardrum.
questions.explanation: "Tube" is already in the label. Copy the spelling exactly.

lesson.title: Final review — putting every skill together
lesson.text: This final set combines the main challenges of Diagram Label Completion: labels that give a name, a function or a measurement; passage paragraphs that do not follow the diagram's order; similar parts close together; alternative names; and numbers with units. Work systematically: study the diagram and the given labels, locate each part in the passage using position words, decide what kind of answer each gap needs, and check the word limit and spelling of every answer.
lesson.example: Label: "mast: up to (1) ______ high". Passage: "The masts are usually 30 metres tall, although some reach 45 metres." Answer: 45 metres (the maximum, as "up to" shows).

questions.evidence: On the largest offshore models, each blade is now more than 100 metres long.
questions.explanation: "Exceed" = "more than". 200 metres is the diameter of the rotor, not the length of one blade, and 35 metres was the typical length in 2000.

questions.evidence: the pitch system, which turns each blade around its own length to change the angle at which it meets the wind.
questions.explanation: The pitch system is inside the hub, which is given as a separate label.

questions.evidence: the main shaft drives a gearbox, which increases the speed of rotation around a hundred times.
questions.explanation: The generator receives this faster rotation but does not increase the speed itself.

questions.evidence: the nacelle, a large housing on top of the tower that contains most of the machinery.
questions.explanation: The label is the definition.

questions.evidence: an anemometer, which measures wind speed, and a wind vane, which measures its direction.
questions.explanation: "Anemometer" is already in the label.

questions.evidence: the yaw drive, a set of motors at the top of the tower, to rotate the whole nacelle so that the blades face into the wind again.
questions.explanation: The pitch system changes the angle of the blades, not the direction of the nacelle.

questions.evidence: On land, towers are usually between 80 and 120 metres tall, while offshore they can reach up to 150 metres.
questions.explanation: The label says "offshore", so the land figures are wrong.

questions.evidence: The tower is fixed to a concrete foundation.
questions.explanation: "Concrete" is already in the label.

title: The Slow Success of the Zip

lesson.title: Scanning for names and numbers
lesson.text: In easy short-answer sets, most answers are names, places, dates and numbers, which are easy to spot because they begin with capital letters or are written as figures. Scan for these first, then read the surrounding sentence to check that it matches the question. Remember that there are usually several names and numbers in the passage, and only one fits each question.
lesson.example: Question: "In which city was the first store opened?" Passage: "Founded in Boston, the company opened its first store in Chicago." Answer: Chicago.

questions.q: At which event did Whitcomb Judson first show his invention?
questions.evidence: who presented it at the Chicago World's Fair in 1893.
questions.explanation: "Show" = "presented". The answer is three words, within the limit. The date 1893 is not an event.

questions.q: What type of footwear was the clasp locker designed for?
questions.evidence: designed it to fasten high boots.
questions.explanation: The rubber boots of 1923 were a later product by B.F. Goodrich, not the purpose of the clasp locker.

questions.q: In which country was Gideon Sundback born?
questions.evidence: Gideon Sundback, an engineer born in Sweden.
questions.explanation: He worked for an American company, but he was born in Sweden.

questions.q: How many teeth per inch did Sundback's improved fastener have?
questions.evidence: which he increased from four per inch to ten per inch.
questions.explanation: "Four" was the number before his improvement.

questions.q: What gave the zipper its name?
questions.evidence: named the boots 'Zippers', after the sound the fastener made when it was opened and closed.
questions.explanation: The name came from the sound, not from the company or the boots.

questions.q: Which company makes about half of the world's zips today?
questions.evidence: the Japanese company YKK, which produces around half of all the zips in the world.
questions.explanation: "About" = "around". B.F. Goodrich and the Universal Fastener Company are earlier companies.

lesson.title: Questions that paraphrase the passage
lesson.text: The question rarely repeats the passage word for word. "Sits on the eggs" may appear in the passage as "incubates"; "hatch" may appear as "the chicks emerge". Before you scan, think of other ways of saying the key words in the question, and look for their meaning, not just their form.
lesson.example: Question: "Who looks after the young?" Passage: "The chicks are cared for by both parents." Answer: both parents.

questions.q: Which sense does the kiwi mainly use to find food?
questions.evidence: it relies on its excellent sense of smell to find food.
questions.explanation: "Mainly uses" = "relies on". The kiwi has poor eyesight, so "sight" is wrong.

questions.q: What proportion of the female's body weight can a single egg weigh?
questions.evidence: a single egg can weigh 20 per cent of the female's body weight.
questions.explanation: "Proportion" is a paraphrase for a percentage. The number is followed by "per cent", which counts as part of the number.

questions.q: In most species, which parent sits on the egg?
questions.evidence: In most species, it is the male that incubates the egg.
questions.explanation: "Sits on" = "incubates".

questions.q: How long does it take kiwi eggs to hatch?
questions.evidence: The eggs take around 80 days to hatch.
questions.explanation: "Three weeks" is the time before the chicks leave the nest.

questions.q: Which introduced animal kills the most young kiwi?
questions.evidence: Stoats ... kill more young kiwi than any other predator.
questions.explanation: Cats, dogs and pigs were also introduced, but stoats kill the most.

questions.q: What is the name of the programme that hatches kiwi eggs in safety?
questions.evidence: conservation groups collect eggs from the wild and hatch them in safety, a programme known as Operation Nest Egg.
questions.explanation: The name is exactly three words, within the limit, and must be copied exactly.

lesson.title: ONE WORD answers
lesson.text: When the limit is ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER, you must choose the single most important word. If the passage says "they burned straw and wool" and the question asks for one thing, read the question again: it may exclude one of them ("apart from wool"). Never write two words joined by "and".
lesson.example: Question: "Besides milk, what is added to the mixture?" Passage: "Milk and sugar are added." Answer: sugar.

questions.q: What did the Montgolfier family's business produce?
questions.evidence: whose family owned a successful paper business.
questions.explanation: The question asks what the business produced; the answer is the product.

questions.q: Apart from wool, what did the brothers burn to make smoke?
questions.evidence: burning a mixture of wool and straw.
questions.explanation: "Apart from wool" excludes the first item.

questions.q: How many animals were carried in the balloon at Versailles?
questions.evidence: the balloon carried three animals: a sheep, a duck and a rooster.
questions.explanation: "Eight" is the number of minutes the flight lasted.

questions.q: For how many minutes did the first flight with people last?
questions.evidence: flew for around 25 minutes.
questions.explanation: "Minutes" is in the question, so only the number is needed. "Eight minutes" was the flight with animals.

questions.q: Which gas was used in the balloon of Jacques Charles?
questions.evidence: Jacques Charles flew in a different type of balloon, filled with hydrogen.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: What material are the envelopes of modern hot-air balloons made of?
questions.evidence: modern balloons were developed with envelopes made of nylon.
questions.explanation: The early balloons were made of cloth and paper.

questions.q: Which fuel do the burners of modern balloons use?
questions.evidence: burners that use propane gas.
questions.explanation: "Gas" would not answer "which fuel"; the specific name is required.

lesson.title: Questions about names and terms
lesson.text: Some questions ask for the name of something that the passage describes: "What are the roots that stick out of the mud called?" The passage will usually give the description and the name in the same sentence, linked by words such as "known as", "called" or a comma. The answer is the name, not the description.
lesson.example: Question: "What is the name of the bird's nest?" Passage: "The bird builds a mound of leaves, known as a scrape." Answer: (a) scrape.

questions.q: In roughly how many countries are mangroves found?
questions.evidence: They are found in around 120 countries.
questions.explanation: "Roughly" = "around". 150,000 is the area in square kilometres.

questions.q: Which large animal lives in the Sundarbans?
questions.evidence: the Sundarbans ... is home to the Bengal tiger.
questions.explanation: "Lives in" = "is home to".

questions.q: What is the scientific name for the roots that stick up out of the mud?
questions.evidence: breathing roots, known as pneumatophores, which stick up out of the mud like pencils.
questions.explanation: "Breathing roots" is the ordinary name; the question asks for the scientific name. Prop roots arch out from the trunk.

questions.q: Through which part do some mangroves get rid of salt?
questions.evidence: others release it through their leaves.
questions.explanation: "Get rid of" = "release". Some mangroves filter salt at the roots, but that is not getting rid of it through a part.

questions.q: How much more carbon can mangroves store than tropical rainforest?
questions.evidence: up to four times as much as the same area of tropical rainforest.
questions.explanation: The answer must include "times" to show the comparison.

questions.q: What has been the main reason for the loss of mangroves?
questions.evidence: The main cause has been the clearing of forests to make space for shrimp farms.
questions.explanation: "Main reason" = "main cause". Coastal development, rice fields and wood collection have "also played a part", so they are not the main reason.

lesson.title: "Where", "how soon" and "which part"
lesson.text: Question words such as "where", "how soon" and "which part" ask for different kinds of information from "what". "Where" may need a place in a house, not a country; "how soon" needs a length of time; "which part" needs a part of an object. Match the answer type to the question word before you write anything.
lesson.example: Question: "Where should the medicine be stored?" Passage: "Keep the medicine in a cool cupboard for up to a year." Answer: (in) a cool cupboard.

questions.q: What does a knife damage when it cuts through an onion?
questions.evidence: When a knife cuts through the onion, it damages the cells.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: What type of chemicals does an onion store?
questions.evidence: An onion stores chemicals known as sulphur compounds.
questions.explanation: The enzymes are also inside the cells, but the question asks what the onion stores as chemicals.

questions.q: In which year was the second enzyme discovered?
questions.evidence: In 2002, Japanese scientists discovered that a second enzyme then turns this substance into an irritating gas.
questions.explanation: 2015 is the year tearless onions went on sale.

questions.q: How soon after cutting is the most gas released?
questions.evidence: The amount of gas released reaches its peak about 30 seconds after the onion has been cut.
questions.explanation: "The most gas" = "reaches its peak".

questions.q: What does the reaction discourage from eating onions?
questions.evidence: discourage hungry animals from eating it.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Where should an onion be kept before it is cut?
questions.evidence: keeping the onion in the fridge for half an hour before cutting it is often effective.
questions.explanation: "Where" needs a place. "Half an hour" answers "how long", not "where".

questions.q: Which part of the onion should be cut last?
questions.evidence: Cooks are also advised to cut the root end last.
questions.explanation: "Which part" needs a part of the onion.

lesson.title: Questions with "how many" and "what proportion"
lesson.text: "How many" needs a number; "what proportion" or "what fraction" needs a part of a whole, such as "two-thirds" or "40 per cent". When the passage contains several numbers close together, read each one with the noun that follows it ("500 million neurons", "three hearts") and choose the one that matches the noun in the question.
lesson.example: Question: "What fraction of the students passed?" Passage: "Of the 300 students, three-quarters passed." Answer: three-quarters.

questions.q: How many neurons does an octopus have?
questions.evidence: An octopus has around 500 million neurons.
questions.explanation: "500 million years" in Paragraph A refers to time, not neurons.

questions.q: What proportion of its neurons are in its arms?
questions.evidence: only about a third of them are in its brain. The remaining two-thirds are located in its eight arms.
questions.explanation: "A third" is the proportion in the brain.

questions.q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.evidence: It has three hearts.
questions.explanation: "Eight" is the number of arms.

questions.q: Which metal does the protein in octopus blood contain?
questions.evidence: it uses a protein based on copper, rather than iron, to carry oxygen.
questions.explanation: "Rather than iron" means iron is not used.

questions.q: What are the colour-changing cells in octopus skin called?
questions.evidence: thousands of cells called chromatophores ... which allow it to change colour.
questions.explanation: The question asks for the name of the cells.

questions.q: What did Otto squirt at the lamp?
questions.evidence: squirting water at a bright lamp that he apparently disliked.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: What objects do veined octopuses use to make a shelter?
questions.evidence: veined octopuses carrying coconut shells across the sea floor and later assembling them into a shelter.
questions.explanation: "Make" = "assembling ... into".

lesson.title: "First", "after that" and other limiting words
lesson.text: Medium questions often contain words that limit the answer to one stage or one case: "first", "after that", "the most", "mainly". The passage will usually give information for several stages or cases, and each is a possible distractor. Underline the limiting word in the question and find the sentence where the passage uses the same idea.
lesson.example: Question: "How often is the hedge cut after its first year?" Passage: "The hedge is cut hard in its first year and then trimmed every six months." Answer: every six months.

questions.q: Which country produces around half of the world's cork?
questions.evidence: Portugal alone produces about half of the world's cork.
questions.explanation: Spain produces "most of the rest", not half.

questions.q: At about what age is a cork oak stripped for the first time?
questions.evidence: A cork oak cannot be stripped until it is around 25 years old.
questions.explanation: "Forty years" is the age when stopper-quality cork is produced, not the first stripping.

questions.q: What name is given to the cork from the first harvest?
questions.evidence: The first harvest produces what is known as virgin cork.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: After the first harvest, how often is the bark removed?
questions.evidence: After that, the bark is harvested every nine years.
questions.explanation: "After the first harvest" matches "After that". Do not confuse this with the number of harvests in a tree's life (about fifteen).

questions.q: What tools are used to remove the bark?
questions.evidence: It is done entirely by hand, by skilled workers using axes.
questions.explanation: "By hand" describes the method; "axes" are the tools.

questions.q: What problem caused many wine producers to stop using cork?
questions.evidence: A chemical contamination known as cork taint was spoiling a significant number of bottles ... and many producers switched to plastic stoppers and screw caps.
questions.explanation: "Stop using cork" = "switched to plastic stoppers and screw caps".

questions.q: Which endangered animal lives in the cork forests?
questions.evidence: one of the world's most endangered cats, the Iberian lynx.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match; "cats" alone is too general.

lesson.title: Questions about purpose and cause
lesson.text: Questions such as "Why ...?", "For what purpose ...?" and "What causes ...?" ask for a reason. Short-answer reasons are usually a noun or a short phrase, such as "courtship" or "to attract prey". Look for words such as "to", "in order to", "because", "used for" and "the result of" in the passage.
lesson.example: Question: "For what purpose do the birds sing at dawn?" Passage: "Males sing at dawn to defend their territory." Answer: (to defend their) territory.

questions.q: What percentage of the species observed in the California study could produce light?
questions.evidence: 76 per cent of the species observed between the surface and a depth of four kilometres could produce their own light.
questions.explanation: "Four kilometres" is the depth, not a percentage.

questions.q: What is the name of the enzyme involved in producing the light?
questions.evidence: with the help of an enzyme called luciferase.
questions.explanation: Luciferin is the light-emitting molecule, not the enzyme; the two words look similar, so check carefully.

questions.q: What provides the light in the anglerfish's lure?
questions.evidence: a glowing lure, lit by bacteria.
questions.explanation: "Provides the light" = "lit by".

questions.q: What is the name of the technique used by animals to hide their silhouettes?
questions.evidence: they use to match the brightness of the light coming from the surface, so that their silhouettes disappear. This technique is known as counterillumination.
questions.explanation: "Hide" = "disappear". "Camouflage" is the general purpose; the question asks for the name of the technique.

questions.q: Which colour of light is quickly absorbed by sea water?
questions.evidence: blue light travels furthest in sea water, while red light is absorbed quickly.
questions.explanation: Blue is the colour that travels furthest, the opposite of the question.

questions.q: For what purpose do fireflies mainly use their flashes?
questions.evidence: Fireflies use their flashes mainly for courtship.
questions.explanation: "Purpose" is answered by "for courtship".

questions.q: What causes breaking waves to glow at night?
questions.evidence: waves breaking at night glow blue. This is caused by dinoflagellates.
questions.explanation: "Causes" = "is caused by".

lesson.title: Names of events, organisations and places
lesson.text: History passages contain many proper nouns: names of events ("Black Sunday"), organisations ("the Soil Conservation Service") and places. Questions may describe these rather than name them ("the government agency set up in 1935"). Match the description in the question to the details in the passage, such as the date or purpose, and copy the name exactly, including capital letters.
lesson.example: Question: "What was the name of the treaty signed in 1648?" Passage: "The Peace of Westphalia, signed in 1648, ended the war." Answer: (the) Peace of Westphalia.

questions.q: What had held the soil of the plains in place before settlers arrived?
questions.evidence: the plains had been covered by deep-rooted prairie grasses, which held the soil in place.
questions.explanation: The hyphenated "deep-rooted" counts as one word, so the full phrase is within the limit.

questions.q: Which crop did farmers plant on more land during the First World War?
questions.evidence: During the First World War, wheat prices rose sharply, and farmers ... ploughed even more land to grow wheat.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: What name was given to the day of the worst dust storm?
questions.evidence: The storms reached their peak on 14 April 1935, a day that became known as Black Sunday.
questions.explanation: "Worst" = "reached their peak". The question asks for the name, not the date.

questions.q: About how many people left the Plains states during the 1930s?
questions.evidence: Around 2.5 million people left the Plains states during the 1930s.
questions.explanation: "300,000 tonnes" refers to dust.

questions.q: Which state did many of these people travel to?
questions.evidence: Many travelled west to California.
questions.explanation: Washington and New York are places the dust reached, not the people.

questions.q: Which organisation was set up in 1935 to teach farmers new methods?
questions.evidence: In 1935, it created the Soil Conservation Service ... which taught farmers methods such as contour ploughing.
questions.explanation: The Shelterbelt Project planted trees; it did not teach methods.

questions.q: Approximately how many trees were planted to reduce the effect of the wind?
questions.evidence: planting around 220 million trees in long lines across the plains to break the force of the wind.
questions.explanation: "Reduce the effect" = "break the force".

lesson.title: Technical processes and their terms
lesson.text: When a passage explains a technology, it often names the method and then describes how it works. Questions may ask for the method, the equipment, the material or the by-product. Identify which of these the question wants: "which method", "what does it pass through", "what is the waste called".
lesson.example: Question: "What is the waste from the process called?" Passage: "The process leaves a thick residue, known as slag." Answer: slag.

questions.q: About how many people rely on desalination for at least some of their water?
questions.evidence: around 300 million people around the world depend at least partly on desalination.
questions.explanation: "Rely on" = "depend on". "20,000" is the number of plants.

questions.q: In which region is thermal distillation still common?
questions.evidence: thermal distillation is still common in the countries of the Persian Gulf.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Which method is used most widely today?
questions.evidence: This technology, now the most widely used in the world, is reverse osmosis.
questions.explanation: Distillation is the oldest method, not the most widely used.

questions.q: Through what is the water pumped in this method?
questions.evidence: Sea water is pumped at very high pressure through membranes.
questions.explanation: "High pressure" describes how the water is pumped, not what it passes through.

questions.q: What is the salty by-product of desalination called?
questions.evidence: a by-product called brine, a highly concentrated salty liquid.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: What percentage of household water in Israel comes from the sea?
questions.evidence: In Israel ... around 80 per cent of household water now comes from the sea.
questions.explanation: "97 per cent" is the proportion of the Earth's water that is salty.

questions.q: Which renewable energy source is being used to power some plants?
questions.evidence: by powering plants with solar power.
questions.explanation: Oil and gas are fossil fuels, not renewable sources.

lesson.title: "Who" questions with several people
lesson.text: When a passage mentions several people, each question describes a particular role: the person who had the idea, who designed a later version, who used it first. Read the whole question and match the role, not just the name that appears nearest to the key words. If the limit allows, write the full name as it appears.
lesson.example: Question: "Who built the first working model?" Passage: "Brown proposed the design, but it was his assistant, Clark, who built the first model." Answer: Clark.

questions.q: Who first heard about the need for an automatic checkout system?
questions.evidence: Bernard Silver ... overheard a supermarket executive asking one of the university's deans for a system that could automatically record product information at the checkout.
questions.explanation: "First heard" = "overheard". Woodland heard about it later from Silver.

questions.q: Which system of communication gave Woodland the idea for the barcode?
questions.evidence: He had learned Morse code as a Boy Scout, and he began to think about how its dots and dashes might be turned into a visual code.
questions.explanation: The beach is where he had the idea, not the system that inspired it.

questions.q: What shape did Silver and Woodland give their design to make it readable from any direction?
questions.evidence: To make the code readable from any direction, the two men later formed the lines into a circular design, like a target.
questions.explanation: The UPC pattern was rectangular, but that was Laurer's later design.

questions.q: Apart from small computers, what invention made the barcode practical?
questions.evidence: The technology only became practical after the development of the laser, and of small, cheap computers.
questions.explanation: "Apart from small computers" excludes the second item.

questions.q: Who designed the rectangular pattern used for the UPC?
questions.evidence: The design selected was a rectangular pattern of vertical lines created by George Laurer, an engineer at IBM.
questions.explanation: Woodland worked with Laurer, but Laurer created the UPC design.

questions.q: What was the first product to be scanned with a UPC barcode?
questions.evidence: a shop assistant scanned the first product with a UPC barcode: a packet of chewing gum.
questions.explanation: "A packet of chewing gum" is five words, so write only "chewing gum".

questions.q: What was the QR code originally designed to track?
questions.evidence: It was originally designed to track car parts during manufacturing.
questions.explanation: Payments and menus are later uses.

lesson.title: Answers that are spread over two sentences
lesson.text: Sometimes the key words of the question are in one sentence, and the answer is in the next, linked by a pronoun such as "it", "they" or "this". When you find the key words, read the sentence before and after them as well, and work out what the pronouns refer to.
lesson.example: Question: "What do the young birds eat?" Passage: "The young birds stay in the nest for a month. During this time, they feed only on insects." Answer: insects.

questions.q: Up to how far do some monarchs travel on their journey south?
questions.evidence: some travelling as far as 4,500 kilometres.
questions.explanation: "Up to" = "as far as". The unit must be included.

questions.q: On which type of tree do the butterflies spend the winter?
questions.evidence: on the branches of oyamel fir trees.
questions.explanation: "Trees" is in the question as "type of tree", so "oyamel fir" is enough.

questions.q: In which year were the winter sites discovered?
questions.evidence: Finally, in 1975, two of his volunteers, working in Mexico, found the mountain forests.
questions.explanation: "Forty years" was the length of Urquhart's search, not the date.

questions.q: For how long can the last generation of the summer live?
questions.evidence: The last generation of the summer, however, is different. Its members ... live for up to eight months.
questions.explanation: "Its" refers to the last generation. The other generations live "only a few weeks".

questions.q: Where is the butterflies' internal clock located?
questions.evidence: they correct their direction using an internal clock located in their antennae.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Which predators are warned by the monarch's colouring?
questions.evidence: making them poisonous to birds, and the monarch's bright orange colouring warns predators to leave them alone.
questions.explanation: The predators are identified in the same sentence as birds.

questions.q: What has destroyed much of the milkweed in the American Midwest?
questions.evidence: the loss of milkweed across the American Midwest, where it has been destroyed by herbicides used on farmland.
questions.explanation: Logging and extreme weather affect Mexico, not the Midwest milkweed.

title: The Colour That Built an Industry

lesson.title: Numbers written as words and as figures
lesson.text: Numbers may be written in the passage as figures (10,000) or as words (eighteen), and in the question in the other form. Both are correct in your answer if the meaning is the same. Watch for numbers that appear with "more than", "about" or "only": include them only if they are needed and fit within the word limit.
lesson.example: Question: "How old was the composer when he wrote his first symphony?" Passage: "He completed his first symphony at the age of eight." Answer: eight / 8.

questions.q: From what creatures was Tyrian purple made?
questions.evidence: Tyrian purple, made in the ancient Mediterranean from sea snails.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: How many snails were needed to produce one gram of dye?
questions.evidence: more than 10,000 snails were needed to make a single gram.
questions.explanation: "More than" should be included because the passage gives a minimum, not an exact number; it fits within the limit.

questions.q: What were the insects used to make a red dye called?
questions.evidence: a brilliant red dye made from cochineal, small insects that live on cactus plants.
questions.explanation: "Indigo" was obtained from plants and was blue.

questions.q: How old was William Perkin when he made his discovery?
questions.evidence: an eighteen-year-old chemistry student in London, William Perkin.
questions.explanation: 1856 is the year, not his age.

questions.q: Which medicine was Perkin trying to produce?
questions.evidence: was attempting to make quinine, the only effective treatment for malaria at the time.
questions.explanation: "Mauveine" is what he produced by accident, not what he was trying to make.

questions.q: From what material did the chemicals in his experiment come?
questions.evidence: he experimented with chemicals obtained from coal tar.
questions.explanation: The bark of a South American tree was the natural source of quinine, not the source of Perkin's chemicals.

questions.q: Which country's companies soon led the synthetic dye industry?
questions.evidence: The industry was soon dominated by Germany.
questions.explanation: "Led" = "dominated". Perkin's own factory was in Britain, but the question asks which country's companies soon led the industry.

lesson.title: Questions that ask for a term
lesson.text: Some questions describe a scientific idea and ask for its name: "What term is used for ...?" The passage usually explains the idea in ordinary words and gives the term once, often in brackets, after "known as" or after a comma. Find the explanation that matches the question, then look nearby for the term.
lesson.example: Question: "What term describes the loss of soil by wind and water?" Passage: "Wind and water gradually remove the soil, a process known as erosion." Answer: erosion.

questions.q: Who first recorded the urban heat island effect?
questions.evidence: This effect, known as the urban heat island, was first recorded in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: At what time is the difference between city and countryside temperatures greatest?
questions.evidence: the difference is greatest at night, when it can reach twelve degrees.
questions.explanation: "Over a year" gives the average, not the time of the greatest difference.

questions.q: What term describes a surface's ability to reflect sunlight?
questions.evidence: The ability of a surface to reflect sunlight is called its albedo.
questions.explanation: The question repeats the passage's explanation, so the answer is the term.

questions.q: What name is given to the process by which plants cool the air?
questions.evidence: Plants cool the air around them by releasing water vapour through their leaves, a process called evapotranspiration.
questions.explanation: "Sweating" is a comparison, not the name of the process.

questions.q: About how many deaths did the European heatwave of 2003 cause?
questions.evidence: The European heatwave of 2003 caused around 70,000 deaths.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: Which city has coated its streets in a light grey material?
questions.evidence: Los Angeles has experimented with coating streets in a light grey material.
questions.explanation: Medellín planted green corridors instead.

questions.q: In which Colombian city were green corridors created?
questions.evidence: In Medellín, Colombia, the city authorities created a network of green corridors.
questions.explanation: Copy the spelling of the name from the passage; "Medellin" without the accent is also accepted.

questions.q: By how much did temperatures fall in the areas with green corridors?
questions.evidence: temperatures in these areas had fallen by around 2°C.
questions.explanation: "One to three degrees" is the average difference between cities and countryside.

lesson.title: Revised and outdated information
lesson.text: Hard passages about science often contrast an old belief with a new finding: "It was once thought that ...; however, recent research suggests ...". Questions may ask about either. Read the question carefully for words such as "earlier", "originally", "now" and "recent", and choose the information from the correct time.
lesson.example: Question: "How many planets were once thought to be in the solar system?" Passage: "Until 2006, Pluto was counted as the ninth planet; today there are officially eight." Answer: nine / 9.

questions.q: According to older textbooks, what was the ratio of bacterial cells to human cells?
questions.evidence: For decades, textbooks stated that bacterial cells in the body outnumbered human cells by ten to one.
questions.explanation: "Older textbooks" points to the earlier belief. "One to one" is the revised figure from 2016.

questions.q: About how many bacteria does a typical adult contain, according to the 2016 study?
questions.evidence: a typical adult contains around 38 trillion bacteria and around 30 trillion human cells.
questions.explanation: 30 trillion is the number of human cells.

questions.q: Babies born in which way are first colonised by bacteria from the skin and hospital?
questions.evidence: those born by caesarean section are first colonised by bacteria from the skin and from the hospital environment.
questions.explanation: Babies born naturally acquire bacteria from their mothers.

questions.q: What substances do bacteria produce when they ferment fibre?
questions.evidence: Bacteria ferment the fibre and produce substances called short-chain fatty acids.
questions.explanation: "Short-chain" is hyphenated and counts as one word, so the answer is within the limit.

questions.q: Which bacterium can multiply after antibiotic treatment?
questions.evidence: this allows a dangerous bacterium, Clostridioides difficile, to multiply.
questions.explanation: The spelling of scientific names must be copied exactly.

questions.q: What proportion of recurring infections has been cured by faecal transplants in clinical trials?
questions.evidence: In clinical trials, it has cured around 90 per cent of recurring infections.
questions.explanation: "Proportion" is answered with a percentage.

questions.q: Which group of people has a microbiome that changes with the seasons?
questions.evidence: Studies of the Hadza ... have revealed a far more diverse microbiome ... one that changes with the seasons.
questions.explanation: "City dwellers" are the group used for comparison, whose microbiome is less diverse.

lesson.title: Comparisons and quantities
lesson.text: Hard questions may ask for a comparison ("How much carbon does permafrost contain compared with the atmosphere?") rather than a simple number. The answer is often a phrase such as "twice as much" or "a quarter". Look for comparative language in the passage: "as much as", "times more", "compared with", "a fraction of".
lesson.example: Question: "How large is the lake compared with the old reservoir?" Passage: "The lake is three times the size of the old reservoir." Answer: three times (the size).

questions.q: What proportion of Northern Hemisphere land lies above permafrost?
questions.evidence: It underlies about a quarter of the land in the Northern Hemisphere.
questions.explanation: "Lies above permafrost" is a paraphrase of "permafrost underlies".

questions.q: What is the layer of soil that thaws each summer called?
questions.evidence: Above it lies the active layer, a shallow layer of soil that thaws each summer and refreezes in winter.
questions.explanation: The question gives the description; the answer is the name.

questions.q: How much carbon does permafrost contain compared with the atmosphere?
questions.evidence: around 1,500 billion tonnes of carbon, roughly twice as much as is currently in the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: The question asks for a comparison, not the amount; "1,500 billion tonnes" does not answer "compared with the atmosphere".

questions.q: How fast is the Arctic warming compared with the global average?
questions.evidence: As the Arctic warms, nearly four times faster than the global average.
questions.explanation: "Nearly four times faster" is exactly three words, within the limit.

questions.q: What name is given to a landscape that has collapsed because of melting ice?
questions.evidence: it collapses as the ice melts, producing an uneven landscape ... known as thermokarst.
questions.explanation: "Gateway to the underworld" is a local name for one particular crater.

questions.q: In which region is the Batagaika crater located?
questions.evidence: the Batagaika crater in Siberia.
questions.explanation: Norilsk and the Yamal Peninsula are in northern Russia but are linked to other events.

questions.q: How much diesel was released at Norilsk in 2020?
questions.evidence: releasing around 21,000 tonnes of diesel into rivers.
questions.explanation: The unit must be included.

questions.q: Which disease broke out on the Yamal Peninsula in 2016?
questions.evidence: In 2016, an outbreak of anthrax on the Yamal Peninsula.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

lesson.title: Heavily paraphrased questions
lesson.text: In hard sets, the question may share almost no words with the passage. "Mental tool for finding direction" may refer to a "star compass"; "the part of the canoe through which they felt the waves" may refer to the "hull". Focus on the meaning of each question, predict what kind of answer it needs, and read the relevant paragraph closely rather than scanning for single words.
lesson.example: Question: "What did sailors use to measure speed?" Passage: "A log tied to a knotted rope was thrown overboard, and the knots passing through the sailor's hands were counted." Answer: (a) knotted rope / (a) log.

questions.q: What name is given to the region with Hawai'i, New Zealand and Rapa Nui at its corners?
questions.evidence: the corners of what is called the Polynesian Triangle: Hawai'i in the north, New Zealand in the south-west, and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) in the east.
questions.explanation: This is the name of the whole region.

questions.q: Who believed that the Pacific islands had been settled from South America?
questions.evidence: Thor Heyerdahl sailed a raft ... to support his theory that the islands had been settled from South America.
questions.explanation: "Kon-Tiki" is the name of the raft, not the person.

questions.q: What was the mental map of the horizon used by navigators called?
questions.evidence: dividing the horizon into a mental map known as a star compass.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match; the question uses the passage's description.

questions.q: Through which part of the canoe could navigators feel the swells?
questions.evidence: Experienced navigators could feel the patterns of swells through the hull of the canoe.
questions.explanation: "Sense" = "feel".

questions.q: How far from land do terns usually travel?
questions.evidence: rarely travel more than about 40 kilometres from shore.
questions.explanation: "Usually" paraphrases "rarely ... more than". The unit must be included.

questions.q: What was the name of the canoe that sailed from Hawai'i to Tahiti in 1976?
questions.evidence: a replica voyaging canoe named Hōkūle'a sailed from Hawai'i to Tahiti.
questions.explanation: Copy the spelling of the name exactly; "Hokule'a" without the marks over the vowels is also accepted.

questions.q: Where did the navigator on this voyage come from?
questions.evidence: Mau Piailug, a master navigator from Micronesia.
questions.explanation: Hawai'i was the starting point of the voyage, not the navigator's home.

questions.q: Which plant provides evidence of early contact between Polynesia and South America?
questions.evidence: The sweet potato, a plant native to South America, was being grown in Polynesia long before Europeans arrived.
questions.explanation: The genetic study is further evidence, but it is not a plant.

lesson.title: Abstract terms and practices
lesson.text: Passages about research methods and society use abstract terms for practices and problems, such as "publication bias" or "pre-registration". Questions describe these practices in other words. Read the definition in the passage, compare it carefully with the question, and give the term, which is usually two or three words.
lesson.example: Question: "What is the practice of checking a study before publication called?" Passage: "Before publication, articles are checked by other experts, a process called peer review." Answer: peer review.

questions.q: Who led the project that tried to repeat psychology studies?
questions.evidence: a project led by the psychologist Brian Nosek.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: How many studies did the project attempt to repeat?
questions.evidence: They attempted to repeat 100 studies.
questions.explanation: "270" is the number of researchers, not studies.

questions.q: What percentage of the repeated studies produced significant results?
questions.evidence: only 36 per cent of the repeated studies did so.
questions.explanation: 97 per cent refers to the original studies, not the repeated ones.

questions.q: What is the name of the theory that self-control becomes tired with use?
questions.evidence: the idea that self-control is like a muscle that becomes tired with use, a theory called ego depletion.
questions.explanation: The question paraphrases the passage's definition.

questions.q: What term describes journals' preference for publishing new and surprising effects?
questions.evidence: One is publication bias: journals have traditionally preferred to publish studies that find new and surprising effects.
questions.explanation: "P-hacking" is a practice of researchers, not journals.

questions.q: Below what p-value has a result traditionally been considered significant?
questions.evidence: A result has traditionally been considered significant if its 'p-value' is below 0.05.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: What is the practice of recording hypotheses before collecting data called?
questions.evidence: researchers publicly record their hypotheses and methods before collecting any data, a practice called pre-registration.
questions.explanation: Registered reports are a type of journal article, not the researchers' practice.

questions.q: What type of article allows a journal to accept a study before its results are known?
questions.evidence: Some journals now offer registered reports, in which they agree to publish a study on the basis of its design, before the results are known.
questions.explanation: "Accept" = "agree to publish".

lesson.title: Dense passages with many specific details
lesson.text: Some hard passages are packed with names, dates, numbers and technical terms, all of the same type. Before answering, quickly mark each date and number in the passage and note what it refers to. Then match each question to the right detail by checking every part of the question, not just the key word.
lesson.example: Question: "In which year was the second expedition?" Passage: "The first expedition sailed in 1910; the second, in 1912, reached the pole; a third was planned for 1915." Answer: 1912.

questions.q: What name did Johann Goeze give to tardigrades?
questions.evidence: who called them 'little water bears' because of the way they move.
questions.explanation: The answer is exactly three words.

questions.q: What is the dried, curled-up form of a tardigrade called?
questions.evidence: curl into a dry, barrel-shaped form known as a tun.
questions.explanation: "Cryptobiosis" is the name of the state, not the form of the body. Read the question carefully: "form" points to "tun".

questions.q: What proportion of their body water do tardigrades lose in this state?
questions.evidence: they lose around 97 per cent of the water in their bodies.
questions.explanation: "Proportion" is answered with a percentage.

questions.q: What is the name of the protein that protects tardigrade DNA from radiation?
questions.evidence: a protein, which they named Dsup, meaning 'damage suppressor', that binds to the animal's DNA and shields it from radiation.
questions.explanation: "Damage suppressor" is the meaning of the name, not the name itself.

questions.q: By how much did this protein reduce the damage to human cells from X-rays?
questions.evidence: they suffered around 40 per cent less damage from X-rays.
questions.explanation: "Hundreds of times" refers to the doses of radiation tardigrades can survive.

questions.q: For how long were tardigrades exposed to the vacuum of space in 2007?
questions.evidence: exposed to the vacuum of space for ten days.
questions.explanation: 2007 is the year, which is already in the question.

questions.q: What was the name of the spacecraft that crashed on the Moon in 2019?
questions.evidence: an Israeli spacecraft, Beresheet, crashed on the Moon.
questions.explanation: Copy the spelling exactly.

lesson.title: Final review — putting every skill together
lesson.text: This final set combines all the main challenges of Short Answer questions: many numbers and dates of the same type, paraphrased questions, limiting words ("first", "so far"), names of people and organisations, and a strict word limit. Work systematically: identify the question word and the type of answer, scan for key words and their paraphrases, read the whole sentence, check every part of the question, and write the shortest correct answer.
lesson.example: Question: "How many medals has the team won so far?" Passage: "The team won three medals in its first season and has won eleven in total so far." Answer: eleven / 11 ("so far" matches the total, not the first season).

questions.q: Before atomic clocks, what fraction of an average day was the second defined as?
questions.evidence: the second was officially defined as 1/86,400 of the average length of a day.
questions.explanation: "Before atomic clocks" points to the old definition in Paragraph A, not the 1967 definition.

questions.q: Who built the first accurate atomic clock?
questions.evidence: In 1955, the physicist Louis Essen built the first accurate atomic clock.
questions.explanation: This is a direct match.

questions.q: At which organisation was the first accurate atomic clock built?
questions.evidence: at the National Physical Laboratory in Britain.
questions.explanation: "Britain" is the country; the question asks for the organisation.

questions.q: In which year was the second redefined using caesium atoms?
questions.evidence: in 1967 the international scientific community redefined the second as the time taken for exactly 9,192,631,770 oscillations of radiation from a caesium atom.
questions.explanation: 1955 is when the first clock was built; 1972 is when leap seconds began.

questions.q: How far out of position would a receiver be because of an error of one millionth of a second?
questions.evidence: an error of just one millionth of a second would place a receiver around 300 metres from its true position.
questions.explanation: The unit must be included.

questions.q: How many leap seconds have been added so far?
questions.evidence: So far, 27 have been added.
questions.explanation: "61 seconds" is the length of a minute that includes a leap second.

questions.q: By which year are leap seconds due to be abolished?
questions.evidence: in 2022 the international body responsible for measurement decided to abolish them by 2035.
questions.explanation: 2022 is when the decision was made, not the deadline.

questions.q: Which element is used in some optical clocks?
questions.evidence: optical clocks, use atoms of elements such as strontium.
questions.explanation: Caesium is used in the older atomic clocks.
